claim: A multi-DOF Cartesian impedance controller can conditionally enforce chosen robot kinetic-plus-spring-energy and controller-power thresholds by uniformly reducing co-stiffness and increasing joint damping, while joint energy tanks are used to preserve passivity during online gain scaling; the demonstrated consequence is increased tracking error, and the results do not establish universal human safety.
epistemic_status: Primary analytical and hardware study with author-reported controller derivation, passivity claim, one-robot experiments, and a simulation; safety implications remain conditional on the selected energy/power metrics, thresholds, model assumptions, and tested setting.
problem_and_setting: Collaborative robot Cartesian impedance control requiring compliance and stability while explicitly limiting controller power and the robot-plus-virtual-spring energy. The implementation targets a 7-DOF KUKA LWR 4+ operated through FRI/ROS and extends an earlier 1-DOF safety-aware controller to multiple degrees of freedom.
method_or_mechanism: The baseline controller combines a screw-theoretic Cartesian virtual spring with joint damping. A scalar lambda uniformly scales the initial Cartesian co-stiffness matrices so robot kinetic energy plus scaled spatial-spring potential does not exceed Emax. A scalar beta scales joint damping so controller-to-robot power does not exceed Pmax. Because online parameter changes can inject internal energy and violate passivity, one port-Hamiltonian energy tank per joint mediates controller action: tank energy supplies action above a lower bound, negative controller power may refill tanks, bounded residual action is retained at depletion, and noise-driven refill is suppressed.
content_summary: The paper derives energy- and power-aware impedance-gain scaling for a multi-DOF manipulator and adds per-joint energy tanks to address passivity under time-varying gains. Hardware experiments track a four-second Cartesian sinusoid using translational stiffness 1000I3, rotational stiffness 100I3, joint damping 50I7, Emax=1.0 J, and Pmax=2.0 W. Enabling limits keeps plotted energy and power near their thresholds but worsens tracking; manual human forces further increase error. A separate simulation applies a -10 N tool force for one second at t=15 s, showing tank refill and disrupted y tracking. The authors identify finite tank energy as an autonomy constraint and propose task-energy-aware sizing or management.
synthesis_role: Mechanism and bounded empirical evidence for explicit energy/power-constrained impedance control with passivity-oriented energy tanks; useful for identifying the performance-versus-limit tradeoff and the gap between metric enforcement and biomechanically validated safety.
development_link: Extends the authors' prior 1-DOF safety-aware impedance controller to a multi-DOF KUKA LWR 4+ using screw-theoretic Cartesian stiffness/co-stiffness, robot kinetic and spatial-spring energy, scalar multi-axis gain scaling, and per-joint energy tanks.

evidence.finding: When kinetic-plus-spring energy exceeds Emax, scalar lambda reduces all initial co-stiffness matrices; when controller power exceeds Pmax, scalar beta increases joint damping. The authors formulate these adaptations to keep the selected energy and power quantities within their prescribed bounds.

The authors state that online parameter scaling can generate internal energy and break passivity, and introduce one port-Hamiltonian energy tank per joint with transmission ratios, depletion handling, and refill rules; they claim the modified interconnected system remains passive.

On the KUKA LWR 4+, plotted energy and power remain at the chosen 1.0 J and 2.0 W thresholds when limits are enabled, while tracking errors increase. Reported translation/orientation mean(SD) errors are 0.0220(0.0076)/0.2790(0.1619) with limits off, 0.0293(0.084)/0.2985(0.1548) with limits on, and 0.0795(0.1143)/0.3216(0.1645) during manual human interaction with limits on.

In simulation, a -10 N tool force applied for one second at t=15 s raises tank energies and disrupts y tracking. Tanks start at 12 J and decline principally for joints 1 and 3, while joint 2 is nearly stationary; increased damping makes controller power negative as intended.

The authors conclude that stiffness/damping scaling enforces the selected limits and that energy tanks decouple and passivate the controller, while acknowledging that finite tank energy limits autonomy and motivates future task-aware tank sizing and management.

evidence.locator: Sec. V–VI and study design described in supplied full text
evidence.finding: The experiments demonstrate threshold regulation and associated tracking degradation in a narrow setup, but do not validate that 1 J and 2 W prevent injury or generalize to other users, contacts, trajectories, robots, or tasks.

boundary_conditions: Demonstrated on one KUKA LWR 4+ configuration using FRI/ROS.
Hardware evaluation uses one four-second Cartesian sinusoidal trajectory and the stated gains.
Chosen limits are Emax=1.0 J and Pmax=2.0 W; their biomechanical safety meaning is not validated.
All initial Cartesian co-stiffness matrices are scaled by a common scalar lambda, constraining adaptation structure.
Power limiting operates by damping scaling and can degrade motion tracking.
Passivity-mediated action depends on finite per-joint tank energy and lower-bound/depletion logic.
Human interaction evidence is an informal manual-force demonstration, not a controlled cohort or collision study.
Tank response to a -10 N, one-second tool force is simulation evidence rather than hardware evidence.
assumptions: Robot kinetic energy and virtual-spring potential are suitable safety-relevant quantities for the intended setting.
Controller-to-robot power is an appropriate quantity to constrain through damping adaptation.
The modeled robot dynamics, Cartesian spring construction, and measured or estimated states are sufficiently accurate for computing the regulated quantities.
Scalar co-stiffness and damping scaling is acceptable despite reduced tracking performance and limited directional selectivity.
The energy-tank interconnection and stated transmission/refill rules satisfy the conditions required by the authors' passivity argument.
Passivity and compliance contribute to safer interaction but are not equivalent to validated injury prevention.
Selected energy and power thresholds must be supplied appropriately for the task and user.

reported: Enforcing energy and power limits increases Cartesian tracking error because stiffness is reduced and damping is increased.
External interaction disrupts y-axis tracking in the simulated force-disturbance case.
Tank energy is finite and caps usable controller energy, thereby limiting autonomy.
Joints that perform more control work consume more tank energy, while a nearly stationary joint consumes little.
inferred: Uniform scalar stiffness scaling may be conservative and cannot independently allocate energy limits by Cartesian direction.
Tank depletion can constrain task completion or sustained autonomous motion even with bounded residual action.
The evidence does not show that the selected 1 J and 2 W limits prevent injury.
Generalization is weak because there is no cohort, statistical hypothesis test, collision study, injury-biomechanics validation, comparison baseline, or diverse task/contact evaluation.
The reported limits regulate selected model-based metrics rather than establishing universal robot safety.
